Sojourner Truth. In May 1851, she rose to speak at the Akron Women's Rights Convention in Ohio and delivered an extemporaneous speech that fused abolitionist and feminist rhetoric, challenging both racism and sexism with searing directness.

Truth testified to her own strength. She had plowed and planted, she said. She had gathered crops into barns. No man could head her. And she asked the question that became her signature refrain: "Ain't I a woman?" She challenged the paternalism of an ideology that placed women on pedestals—women who believed themselves too delicate for labor. Her testimony proved that Black women's strength and capability made them equal to any man.

The speech was reconstructed and published by Frances Dana Gage under the title "Ain't I a Woman?" with dialect speech that may not reflect Truth's actual words. Yet it became central to twentieth-century Black feminist theory. Truth addressed both white women, questioning their understanding of Black women's experience, and white men, exposing their justifications for oppression. Her testimony invoked the framework of intersectionality long before the term existed, asserting the humanity and dignity of Black women—a voice that would shape Black feminism for generations.
